cards.q: What is the core morphologic definition of papulosquamous disorders?
cards.a: They are conditions defined by the presence of **erythematous papules and plaques** topped by **surface scales (squames)**.

cards.q: What are the two principal prototype conditions of the papulosquamous spectrum?
cards.a: **Psoriasis** and **Lichen Planus**.

cards.q: What is the clinical definition of psoriasis?
cards.a: A **chronic, non-infectious, scaly, erythematous** skin disease.

cards.q: What is the prevalence of psoriasis in the general population?
cards.a: Approximately **1-2%**.

cards.q: In which season does psoriasis typically show exacerbations?
cards.a: In the **colder winter months**.

cards.q: List the components of Metabolic Syndrome often associated with psoriasis.
cards.a: **Visceral Obesity**, **Insulin Resistance**, **Hypertension**, **High Triglycerides**, and **Low HDL-Cholesterol**.

cards.q: What systemic surveillance protocol is mandatory for psoriatic patients?
cards.a: Lifelong periodic screening for **hypertension**, **diabetes mellitus**, and complete **fasting lipid profiles**.

cards.q: What is the fundamental cellular defect in psoriasis?
cards.a: Accelerated mitotic division (**hyperproliferation**) in the **basal cell layer**.

cards.q: How much does the epidermal turnover time decrease in psoriasis?
cards.a: From the normal **28 days** down to **7 days**.

cards.q: Which immune cells are responsible for the immunologic cascade driving psoriatic proliferation?
cards.a: Activated **CD4+** and **CD8+ T-lymphocytes**.

cards.q: What role does ultraviolet (UV) radiation play in psoriasis?
cards.a: UV radiation induces **immunosuppression** of epidermal T-cells; lack of exposure (e.g., winter) precipitates flares.

cards.q: Which infection is specifically linked to the initiation of guttate psoriasis?
cards.a: **Hemolytic Streptococcal infection** (often 1-3 weeks prior to eruption).

cards.q: Which classes of drugs are known to exacerbate or trigger psoriasis?
cards.a: **Antihypertensives** (beta-blockers, Ca channel blockers, ACE inhibitors), **NSAIDs**, and **anti-malarial drugs**.

cards.q: Define the Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response).
cards.a: The development of psoriatic plaques on **previously uninvolved skin** following **trauma** (e.g., friction, incisions, excoriation).

cards.q: What is the Auspitz sign?
cards.a: The appearance of **pinpoint bleeding spots** upon mechanical removal (scraping) of psoriatic scales due to the unroofing of dilated dermal capillaries.

cards.q: How does the Auspitz sign differ from the Carpet-tack sign?
cards.a: Auspitz sign is related to **psoriasis**; Carpet-tack sign is related to **follicular plugging** in **Discoid Lupus Erythematosus**.

cards.q: What are the typical clinical features of Psoriasis Vulgaris?
cards.a: **Bilateral and symmetrical** scaly erythematous plaques, typically on **extensor surfaces** (elbows, knees), scalp, and lumbosacral area.

cards.q: List four common nail findings in psoriasis.
cards.a: **Pitting**, **subungual hyperkeratosis**, **ridges**, and **onycholysis**.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of nail psoriasis?
cards.a: It carries a very strong association with **psoriatic arthritis**; joint screening is mandatory.

cards.q: Why is flexural (inverse) psoriasis often misdiagnosed?
cards.a: Because scaling is reduced or absent due to moisture/friction, leading it to be mistaken for **Candidiasis**, **tinea cruris**, or **bacterial intertrigo**.

cards.q: What characterizes guttate psoriasis?
cards.a: Abrupt, **2-5 mm** droplet-like scaly papules, typically following **streptococcal infection**.

cards.q: What percentage of body surface area defines erythrodermic psoriasis?
cards.a: More than **90%** of the body surface area.

cards.q: Why is erythrodermic psoriasis considered a medical emergency?
cards.a: Risk of **hypothermia**, **electrolyte imbalance**, **hypoalbuminemia**, **high-output cardiac failure**, and **sepsis**.

cards.q: What is the histopathologic basis of pustular psoriasis?
cards.a: **Sterile intraepidermal** collections of neutrophils (spongiform pustules of Kogoj).

cards.q: What is a well-known iatrogenic trigger for acute generalized pustular psoriasis?
cards.a: Abrupt withdrawal or systemic administration of **corticosteroids**.

cards.q: What is the most common joint involvement in psoriatic arthritis?
cards.a: **Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints**.

cards.q: What is the concern with Coal Tar use in psoriasis?
cards.a: Pungent malodor, irritant potential, **black staining**, and it should not be used on face, genitalia, flexures, or in pustular psoriasis.

cards.q: What is the risk of prolonged continuous topical corticosteroid use for psoriasis?
cards.a: Triggering **severe rebound flares** or conversion to **acute generalized pustular psoriasis**.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Salicylic acid 5% in psoriasis?
cards.a: It acts as a **keratolytic agent** by dissolving intercellular desmosomes to facilitate penetration of other topicals.

cards.q: How does Calcipotriol work?
cards.a: It is a **Vitamin D3 analogue** that binds the VDR to halt basal hyperproliferation, induce differentiation, and suppress pro-inflammatory T-cell cytokines.

cards.q: What is the dose and administration rule for Methotrexate in psoriasis?
cards.a: **0.2-0.4 mg/kg/week**, administered as a **single weekly dose** (never daily).

cards.q: What are the major side effects and monitoring requirements for Methotrexate?
cards.a: Side effects: **liver/bone marrow toxicity**, **teratogenicity**. Monitoring: **CBC** and **LFTs** monthly.

cards.q: What is the strict timeline for avoiding pregnancy with Acitretin (Retinoids)?
cards.a: Pregnancy must be avoided during and for **3 years after** the end of treatment.

cards.q: What is the 'Classic 6 Ps' mnemonic for Lichen Planus?
cards.a: **Pruritic**, **Polygonal**, **Planar**, **Purple**, **Polished**, **Papules/Plaques**.

cards.q: What specific viral infection is associated with Lichen Planus?
cards.a: **Hepatitis C Virus (HCV)**.

cards.q: What are Wickham striae?
cards.a: Reticulate white streaks forming a network, characteristic of **mucosal lichen planus**.

cards.q: What is the characteristic feature of Actinic Lichen Planus?
cards.a: Occurs on **sun-exposed areas**, flares in **summer** and remits in **winter** (opposite of psoriasis).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic significance of Pterygium Unguis in Lichen Planus?
cards.a: It is **virtually pathognomonic**; involves fusion of the proximal nail fold with the nail bed, resulting in permanent nail loss.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of Pityriasis Rosea?
cards.a: Starts with a single **Herald patch**, followed by multiple crops of oval scaly lesions on the trunk/proximal limbs in a **Christmas tree pattern**.

cards.q: Which viruses are linked to the etiology of Pityriasis Rosea?
cards.a: **HHV-6** and **HHV-7**.

cards.q: What is the expected resolution time for Pityriasis Rosea?
cards.a: Spontaneous healing within **4-8 weeks**.

cards.q: How does the distribution of Pityriasis Rosea compare to psoriasis and lichen planus?
cards.a: Pityriasis Rosea follows **Langer's cleavage lines** (Christmas tree pattern) on the trunk/proximal limbs; Psoriasis prefers **extensors**; Lichen Planus prefers **flexors**.

cards.q: Which condition is characterized by pigmentary incontinence and slate-gray to dark-brown macular stains?
cards.a: **Lichen Planus**.

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for localized Lichen Planus?
cards.a: **High-potency topical corticosteroids**.
